analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal handgun background checks and the semiautomatic assault weapons ban.
analysis.headline: Sole-sponsored with zero cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe three gun laws off the books: the Brady Act, which created a waiting period and then a national instant background check for handgun buyers; the 1994 ban on manufacturing and possessing semiautomatic assault weapons; and a 1993 law governing federal firearms licenses. It would also erase every penalty and forfeiture already imposed under those laws, so pending enforcement cases could not go forward. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee but never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun owners would no longer face the Brady waiting period or a background check to buy a handgun, and could again legally buy semiautomatic assault weapons and the parts banned in 1994. Firearms manufacturers and dealers would regain a market for products the 1994 law barred them from making and would no longer run buyers through the federal check. Anyone facing penalties or forfeitures under the repealed laws would have those liabilities extinguished.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Brady Act, ending the waiting period before a handgun purchase and the national instant background check system.
Repeals the 1994 ban on manufacturing, transferring, or possessing semiautomatic assault weapons, making those firearms legal to make and own again.

Extinguishes every liability, penalty, and forfeiture already incurred under the repealed laws and bars any pending prosecution from being sustained — people charged under the Brady Act or the assault weapons ban would go free.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on communities affected by gun violence: with no background check, waiting period, or federal licensing rules, people legally barred from buying handguns — including those with felony records — could purchase them without any screening. Law enforcement also loses the background-check system and the enforcement tools created by the repealed laws, and cases already brought under them would collapse.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Brady Act removes the only federal screening of handgun buyers, so people legally prohibited from owning guns — such as those with felony convictions — could buy handguns with no check and no waiting period.

The bill does not merely repeal the laws going forward: it retroactively extinguishes penalties and forfeitures already incurred and blocks pending prosecutions, erasing consequences for violations that already happened.
Repealing the Federal Firearms License Reform Act of 1993 strips away the federal licensing and record-keeping framework for gun dealers, making it harder to trace firearms used in crimes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Gun owners would gain real legal freedom: no waiting period, no background check, and re-legalized semiautomatic firearms. The price is removing the screening system that keeps handguns from people legally barred from buying them, dismantling dealer licensing and record-keeping, and retroactively nullifying penalties already imposed. That trade-off was never debated — the bill drew no cosponsors and no committee hearing, so Congress never weighed it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee in June and July 1998, and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on June 24, 1998, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on July 2, 1998 to the Subcommittee on Crime.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Brady background checks and the assault weapons ban stayed in force; gun-control supporters and law enforcement kept the existing laws, while gun owners and the firearms industry gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no member of either party cosponsored it.

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Campaigned through the 1990s to repeal the 1994 assault weapons ban and the Brady waiting period, the two laws this bill targeted.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary (Chair Henry Hyde)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearms law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 1998, sent it to the Subcommittee on Crime, and never scheduled a hearing or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever held; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never became a partisan test.

industries.note: Repealing the assault weapons ban re-opens a product line the industry has been barred from making since 1994, and repealing the Brady Act ends the background checks and waiting period dealers run buyers through. The industry's gain comes from removing the screening the public's safety depends on.

The Brady Act's instant background check system and the penalties under the repealed laws are tools police and prosecutors use to keep guns from prohibited buyers; the bill repeals them and extinguishes cases already brought.
